This is expressed in a remarkable report (khabar) of a saying of the Prophet about the Ahl al-jinnat, the inhabitants of paradise, which Mulla Sadra quotes in full. “An Angel comes to the inhabitants of paradise and, with their permission, enters their dwelling. After entering and greeting them on God’s behalf, he presents them with a letter from God. The letter speaks to each human being. It says: ‘From the Ever-Living, who never dies, to the ever-living, who never dies.

“And now, to continue: Truly, I say to a thing, “Be!” and it is’ (2:117 and elsewhere). ‘Today I make you someone who can say to a thing, “Be!” and it is.’” The Prophet then explained: “Thus no inhabitant of paradise says to a thing, ‘Be!’ without its coming into being.” There could hardly be a more beautiful image of creative Imagination.

Mulla Sadra’s exposition continues naturally by developing a celebrated passage from Ibn Arabi on himma: spiritual energy concentrated in the heart, which gives the heart’s intentions the effective power of creative Imagination. “Through his faculty of representation,” Ibn Arabi writes, “everyone creates within his imagination things that exist nowhere but in that faculty. This is the general and ordinary case.

“But through his himma the gnostic creates something that exists outside the seat of this faculty, while his himma continues to sustain it, for maintaining what he has created costs it no effort.” A comparison between Ibn Arabi’s and Mulla Sadra’s teachings on the creative power of imagination would require an entire book. None of the great fundamental themes would be absent: the witness encountered in contemplation (shâhid), the Perfect Human Being (Insân Kâmil, anthropos teleios)—themes also evoked in this Gloss by Mulla Sadra himself.
6. The Three Stages of Human Growth

In Book V of the second part of his Eastern Theosophy (§ 247 of our edition), Suhrawardi offers this testimony: “I have undergone authentic experiences within myself which prove that there are four worlds.” As his commentator Qutb al-Din Shirazi (d. 710/1311) explains, this scheme comprises: (1) the world of the Victorious Lights (Anwâr qâhira), or cherubic Intelligences—the Jabarut; (2) the world of Lights that each serve as the Espahbad, the governing spiritual power, of a celestial or human body.

We have already noted the correspondence between this ancient Iranian term associated with chivalry and the Stoic hegemonikon, the ruling faculty. This is the world of angelic souls, Animae caelestes and Animae humanae—the Malakut; (3) the world of the two kinds of barzakh: the realm of the Elements and that of the astronomical Heavens.

In Suhrawardi’s vocabulary, barzakh can mean anything made of physical matter that screens or obstructs the light; it does not refer only to the eschatological intermediate world, the 'âlam al-Mithâl, as it does in the present discussion (see note 138 above); and (4) the 'âlam al-Mithâl itself, the world of self-subsisting Images, possessing all the richness of the sensory world but existing without matter.

We recover Mulla Sadra’s threefold scheme simply by placing the 'âlam al-Mithâl, the mundus imaginalis or imaginal world, within the Malakut, the world of the Soul: (1) the spiritual world of pure Intelligences ('âlam al-'Aql); (2) the psycho-spiritual world of the Soul, or world of imaginative consciousness ('âlam al-khayâl, mundus imaginalis); and (3) the material world of sensory perception ('âlam al-hiss).

Understood in this way, the world of imaginative consciousness, or of the Soul, lies between the sensory and intelligible worlds. It acts as their meeting ground, the intermediate world (barzakh), sharing in the nature of both. It corresponds to what Swedenborg called the world of apparentiae reales, appearances that are real. Suhrawardi assigns this intermediate world a threefold role: “It is through this world that the resurrection of bodies, divine appearances, and all the events spoken of in prophecy take place” (§ 248).

We have already pointed out that, without such a world, our philosophers would no longer be able to speak of resurrection in its true sense, account for visionary experience, or even practice ta'wil, the spiritual interpretation of divine revelation. They could no longer grasp the spiritual meaning of the revealed texts—that is, the meaning and reality of events that are not physical, but are “events in Heaven.” When the intermediate world disappears from view, so do all three functions it makes possible. Its disappearance is also a sign that the threefold understanding of the worlds, which it holds together, has already been lost.
The three worlds can also be called, in order, “this world” (donyâ), the “intermediate world” (barzakh), and the “world beyond” (âkhira).

We shall use these terms for the remainder of our discussion. Their threefold structure corresponds to that of the human being: body (jism, hylê), soul (nafs, psychê), and spirit (rûh, pneuma). Losing sight of the intermediate world (mundus imaginalis) goes hand in hand with a diminished understanding of the human being: the threefold structure is reduced to two terms, or even to the dualism of spirit (or soul, treated as its equivalent) and body. We have recalled that the second Council of Constantinople, in 869 CE, excluded the threefold scheme from official Christian anthropology.
What is called the dualism of body and soul—extension and thought—with all its difficulties, has its origins in a decision of this kind.

By contrast, Mulla Sadra’s threefold scheme, shared by his predecessors and successors, is readily recognizable as the anthropology of Gnosis, which distinguishes human beings according to the bodily, psychic, and spiritual levels of existence—the hylic, psychic, and pneumatic.

In fact, Mulla Sadra’s entire teaching on resurrection reaches its culmination through this scheme: the idea that a human being undergoes three births and three stages of growth. We have already encountered this idea repeatedly, because it is connected with every threefold pattern discussed so far.

Of the intermediate world’s three functions, Mulla Sadra is especially concerned here with its role as the world through which the resurrection of bodies becomes possible. The “imaginal body” (jism mithâlî), understood as a body acquired by the soul itself (jism moktasab), links the three elements of the human being and allows us to understand the literal spiritual meaning of the resurrection of bodies.
The first resurrection takes place when a human being leaves the mother’s womb and enters the sensory world: the birth of the physical human being.

The second takes place when a person departs from this material, sensory world and enters the intermediate world of the Soul. This is the Qiyâmat soghrâ, the “Lesser Resurrection.” It is the time spent in the barzakh, a time which, in relation to the transformations still to come, is no more than the “time of the cradle.”

The theme of resurrection is heard a third time, at a higher octave, in the Qiyâmat kobrâ, the “Greater Resurrection”: a cosmic event and the birth of the human being into a higher plane of existence. This is the passage from the Soul’s intermediate world to the world of cherubic Intelligences, in which the psychic or psycho-spiritual human being grows into a pneumatic—that is, fully spiritual—human being. The whole process can be read both as a prophetic history yet to unfold and as the pattern of a journey of spiritual initiation.

Three worlds, then, correspond to the three levels of human reality. Resurrection takes place through three mediating acts: that of Azrael, the Angel of Death, and the first and second calls of Seraphiel’s Trumpet (39:68). Gloss 629 (lithographed edition, p. 518) brings together Mulla Sadra’s magnificent vision, embracing every level of the worlds, from the Elements and minerals to the angelic realm and still-unrevealed universes. All are set in motion by the same restlessness of being, the same act of existence forever ascending.

“We have already explained to you,” he says, “that God has unfolded the structure of existence into three worlds: this world (donyâ), the intermediate world (barzakh), and the world beyond (âkhira). In relation to this world, He created the material body; in relation to the intermediate world, the Soul; and in relation to the world beyond, the Spirit or Intelligence. He has also established three intermediaries through which the transfer to each world takes place: the Angel of Death; the blast of the Trumpet announcing the ‘Last Hour’ (nafakhat al-qar', see 101:1 ff.); and the ‘blast of the Trumpet that strikes with a blinding flash’ (39:68).

“Death concerns material bodies; the Trumpet announcing the Last Hour concerns Souls; the Trumpet of the blinding flash concerns Spirits.” In other words, through death, through departure from the physical world, human nature rises from this material world into the world of the Soul. From the world of the Soul it rises into the world of Spirit. And through the world of Spirit, it will rise into universes of which we have no inkling—universes whose divine Names, destined to be revealed within them, have themselves not yet been revealed.

“As long as a human being is present in this world,” Mulla Sadra continues, “the condition under which he becomes visible corresponds to the nature of the material body. It is the body that appears, and through it practical deeds are done and effects produced. Soul and Spirit are enfolded within the body’s existence, both hidden beneath its veil; and it is through the body that they receive what sustains them (amdâdât). When God wishes to transfer the soul from this world to the intermediate world (barzakh), He causes the body to die through the Angel of Death. This departure is the Qiyâmat soghrâ, or Lesser Resurrection.

“Now, born into the intermediate world, the soul begins its second growth, the growth proper to a soul (nash'at thâniya nafsânîya). It is now the soul that becomes manifest and visible; the soul that can produce effects in the intermediate world; the soul that directly receives what sustains it, and through which this sustenance reaches its spirit (rûh, pneuma) and its body—the body it has acquired (jism moktasab), its resurrection body. For the soul is what appears in the intermediate world, and there it shapes its own Form: its subtle, psycho-spiritual body, corresponding to its character, its ways of being and acting.

“The intermediate world, the barzakh, is therefore a distinct world between this world and the world beyond. It is the ‘Lasting Abode’ (dâr al-qarâr, 40:42), enduring as the dawn endures between night and day. It is the dwelling of the Souls and Spirits transferred from this world since the beginning of time, and of those who will continue to be transferred until the end of time, when the Last Hour sounds—the hour of the Great Upheaval (al-Tammât al-kobrâ, 79:34).”

The soul’s growth in the intermediate world is thus its second growth, arising out of the life it has lived in this world. That is why the intermediate world, the barzakh, contains both a paradise and a hell. Through the body it has formed for itself by its deeds (jism moktasab), the soul already becomes one or the other. As we know, the power through which it gives substance to this body is its imagination. This is what gives meaning to the saying quoted earlier: “For the one who dies, resurrection begins at the moment of death.”

Just as the Soul occupies a position between the world of Spirit and the world of the body, the intermediate world receives influences from both. We have also just seen that this intermediate state has a duration, which will end when our aeon—our cosmic age—comes to its close. That ending brings the Greater Resurrection: the soul’s passage from the intermediate world to the abode of Haqîqat, the Real or Truth, where the act of being attains the full truth of its own essence.
Here Mulla Sadra’s indications become somewhat tangled, as he moves from one Quranic verse to another, each requiring its own ta'wil, or spiritual interpretation.

First he reminds us that “one day of God” is equivalent to a thousand of our years (22:46). A week of such days therefore equals seven thousand years. If a week is then allotted to each of those days, the result is a week of weeks—forty-nine thousand years. In human reckoning, this represents the number of years contained in a complete divine day. “The Angels and the Spirit ascend in a day whose duration is fifty thousand years” (70:4).

The fiftieth millennium then corresponds to the millennium of the Mahdi: in Shiite terms, the Parousia, the coming of the Twelfth Imam, the Hidden Imam. The same number is also known in Ismaili Gnosis, where it is connected with a “cycle of epiphany.” The final millennium is the reign of the Qâ'im al-Qiyâmat, the Imam who prepares the Resurrection. The reign of the Qa'im thus prepares the Event that will bring the cycle of our aeon to an end.

In the language of “events in Heaven,” the ending of our aeon marks the passage from the intermediate world to the world beyond (âkhira): from the world of the Soul to the world of Spirit. The Lesser Resurrection was the soul’s passage from this world into the intermediate world known as the “eighth clime,” the world of the mystical cities of Hurqalya, Jabalqa, and Jabarsa. It is in this same intermediate world that the Greater Resurrection will take place. This tells us how the events of the last things, announced in the Quran and the hadiths, are to be read and understood in their concrete spiritual meaning.

The “eighth clime,” the intermediate world, is the world in which the Soul’s events take place; and the history of the Soul, viewed from this world, is metahistory—a history beyond the conditions of ordinary historical time. Imaginative consciousness perceives the events of this metahistory. Every perception of events concerning the Resurrection and the final destiny of the soul presupposes this metahistorical dimension.

On the other hand, Mulla Sadra seems to identify the blast of the Trumpet announcing the Last Hour (nafakhat al-qar', see 101:1 ff.) with the first blast of the Trumpet of the blinding flash (nafakhat al-sa'aq, see 39:68). This blast announces the completion of the fifty thousand years. We have shown elsewhere that, in the theology of the Shaykhi school, the first blast of Seraphiel’s Trumpet symbolizes a breath that draws everything in the universe back into itself, beginning a great cosmic pause.

The second blast symbolizes the breath that sends everything forth again, bringing about the restoration—the apokatastasis—of all beings to their original wholeness. Here we must conceive the passage from the intermediate world to the world of Haqîqat by analogy with the passage out of this world into the intermediate world. The blinding flash of the first blast of Seraphiel’s Trumpet overwhelms the souls in the intermediate world; the second raises them into the world beyond (see 39:68).

Having completed its growth in the intermediate world, the soul dies to that world, as though undergoing a new initiation, so that it may be reborn into the world of Spirit and the cherubic Intelligences. Then begins its new growth as Spirit (nash'at rûhânîya 'aqlîya). A Quranic verse announces it: “Then He will bring forth another creation” (29:19).

This new growth answers a need of the supreme Spirit, which longs for the ever-greater unfolding of its own revelation. It calls for increasingly perfect forms of manifestation (mazâhir) through which divine Names still unrevealed, hidden, and unknown, may become manifest. The prophetic saying awakens us to these Names: “One day I shall glorify Him by Names that I do not yet know.” Nothing could be further from a return to some supposedly formless state.
Indeed, such a return would contradict more than anything else the longing of the “Hidden Treasure that yearns to be known.”

Because its inspiration is directed toward the final destiny of beings, Mulla Sadra’s philosophy sounds like the culmination of prophetic philosophy. “Then,” he says, “from this more perfect Theophany—a fuller manifestation of God—there unfolds a more magnificent form of manifestation. Through it, divine Names still unrevealed become manifest. As they appear, the cosmic Throne expands and grows. As the Throne expands, so do the circles of the Abode Beyond (Dâr al-Âkhira).

“And as they expand, the human being reaches the fullness of his growth in the world beyond all worlds. It is then the Spirit that is visible and manifest, master of its own powers of action. Through the Spirit, what is needed for existence reaches the soul and the body—the subtle resurrection body, jism moktasab. The believer enters his paradise in a state in which human nature has attained the perfection of its strength.”
Thus the phases of ma'âd jismânî, bodily resurrection, unfold through birth and growth in the intermediate world (barzakh), followed by birth and growth in the world beyond (âkhira).

First, when the soul departs from this world, it rises into the intermediate world with its subtle psycho-spiritual body (caro spiritualis—spiritual flesh): the body it has formed for itself through its being and its actions, and which continues to grow in the intermediate world, the world of the Soul. This is the Qiyâmat soghrâ, the Lesser Resurrection. Then, at the Qiyâmat kobrâ, the Greater Resurrection, the resurrection body attains the stature of a body that is spirit. In this way the body passes through the three states that Mulla Sadra describes elsewhere, corresponding to the three degrees of human reality in the Gnostic view: the bodily human being, the psychic human being, and the spiritual human being.

More than anything else, Mulla Sadra’s philosophy, like Shiite philosophy as a whole, is inspired by the ultimate destiny of the soul. That is also why it has the character of a prophetic philosophy, placing before human choice the prospect of future spiritual rebirths. Anyone who turns toward the worlds our thinkers seem to be pointing out to us cannot help feeling a certain astonishment at the noisy success enjoyed today, in Europe and elsewhere, by an improvised mixture of theology and philosophy built on science and technology. It claims to restore humanity’s “cosmic dimensions,” when in fact it is simply inhuman.

One metaphysician of the traditional school could therefore write, with some humor, that it was a case of “a theology that has succumbed to microscopes and telescopes, to machines and to their philosophical and social consequences.” For Mulla Sadra and those who share his outlook, however, we cannot speak of “cosmic dimensions” so long as we remain within the limits of sensory experience and the physical human being.

Humanity’s cosmic dimensions lie in our belonging to higher worlds, and in our resurrections into them—a belonging that can be understood only through a “commitment” reaching beyond death. Otherwise, however “cosmic” our dimensions and achievements may be, we must remember that neither brings us even a single cubit nearer to the world of the Malakut.

We hope these few pages have conveyed something of the richness of the Glosses that Mulla Sadra wrote in the margins of Suhrawardi’s Eastern Theosophy. What we have said, of course, is only a prelude.

We must still bring their themes and purposes into relation, first, with the immense body of Sadra Shirazi’s work; then with Shiite theosophy as a whole, both Twelver and Ismaili; and finally with the full range of Neoplatonic gnoses and philosophies of divine wisdom. The fact that these traditions are scattered across centuries and books does nothing to weaken their spiritual family resemblance.

“Iran and Gnosis” is not simply a chapter in the history of religions, a reckoning of what belongs to the past. It is a living affinity, sustained from century to century in Islamic Persia, sometimes hidden and sometimes openly expressed. Its meaning is by no means exhausted by its importance in the past, as a merely “historical” phenomenon. Even today, it still holds the promise of new spiritual births.
1. In the Holy City of Qomm, “the Well-Protected”

In the preceding pages, an ecstatic confession by Mîr Dâmâd carried us, in spirit, to the holy city of Qomm, “the Well-Protected” (Qomm al-mahrûsa). We return there now, for we could hardly leave out a portrait of a Shiite thinker whose work may be less extensive and less complete than Mollâ Sadrâ's, but whose depth and originality still inspire devoted followers in Iran today: Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî, whom we have already mentioned many times in this book.

We ourselves devoted several years of teaching to his thought, and we must confess that he is one of those philosophers who exert what can only be called a charm. Perhaps that is because every page of his work quietly vibrates with a genuine personal spiritual experience, one matched by the depth of his philosophical intelligence.

With Qâzî Sa'îd we encounter a tendency within the School of Isfahan somewhat different from that represented by Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî. In Isfahan, Qâzî Sa'îd studied under Mollâ Rajab 'Alî Tabrîzî, whose metaphysics of being sought to meet, in the most uncompromising way, the demands of apophatic theology—the theology that approaches God by denying the applicability of our ordinary descriptions to the divine Essence—as taught by the Imams.

Yet Qâzî Sa'îd also studied in Isfahan under Mohsen Fayz, himself a pupil and son-in-law of Mollâ Sadrâ, whose influence on him was profound. Thus a line of intellectual descent takes shape, though without effacing the distinctive features that we shall shortly describe.

Our philosopher was born in 1049/1639 in “the holy city of Qomm, the Well-Protected.” There he taught, and there he died (1103/1691). His life and work therefore bring before us the presence of a city that is among the great pilgrimage sites of Shiite Islam. This connection is stronger still because one of Qâzî Sa'îd's major achievements was an extensive work of philosophical theology, written as a commentary on the principal book of another eminent figure from Qomm: Ibn Bâbûyeh Qommî, commonly known as Shaykh Sadûq (d. 391/991), one of the pillars of Shiite theology. A bridge is thus thrown across seven centuries, its two supports resting in the fourth/tenth and the tenth/seventeenth centuries.

We can only regret that no comprehensive study of Qomm yet exists—one that would embrace the history of its pilgrimages, monuments, and scholars. Already famous in the pre-Islamic, Zoroastrian Persia of the past , when a stream now long dry still brought cool water to its gardens, Qomm continues to leave a deep impression on the visitor. Of course, one must not go there as a tourist; that would be to miss the point entirely.

To feel the city's presence, one must in some sense have the soul of a pilgrim, a soul capable of resonating with the devotion that has drawn people here, century after century, in search of an “other world.” Qomm offers neither worldly amusements nor secular curiosities. Instead, it is a city of some three hundred mosques—some quite recent, such as the beautiful Borûjardî Mosque—and about five thousand students studying with their teachers in the madrasas of its theological university.

Thoughtful figures or hurried figures pass by, their movements given a natural dignity by the flowing rhythm of the 'abâ, a cape-like mantle with wide sleeves. Countless lights blaze in the sanctuaries. To the pilgrim walking there in the evening, everything seems to offer a foretaste of the hidden splendours of an “other world.” These are the impressions we carry away from Qomm, an age-old place of pilgrimage, in whose covered walks we shall imagine the great theologian Ibn Bâbûyeh alongside his later commentator, Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî.

What connects these two figures is an experience of the soul shared across the centuries. For it was in Qomm's sanctuary that Qâzî Sa'îd himself received certain spiritual visions, which he carefully recorded in his writings; and it was in Qomm that several of his deepest works of spiritual philosophy were inspired .
But there may be something more: a hidden connection between the sacred history of the city itself and the work of our philosopher.

At the beginning of Ibn Bâbûyeh's great book, on which Qâzî Sa'îd wrote his commentary—the Book of Tawhîd, concerning the divine Oneness—stands a long sermon delivered by the Eighth Imam, 'Alî Rezâ (d. 203/818), at Merv before the court of al-Ma'mûn. The latter had inherited from his father, Hârûn al-Rashîd, sovereignty over the eastern part of the Abbasid Empire.

Perhaps influenced by his vizier Fazl ibn Sahl, a Zoroastrian convert to Islam who sympathised strongly with the Persians and the Shiites, al-Ma'mûn had conceived a remarkable plan—remarkable, at least, for an Abbasid ruler. He meant to win over the Shiites by naming their Imam as his future successor. The plan was hardly compatible with the Imam's own understanding of his calling: neither he nor his predecessors had taken part in political agitation, and the conditions required for establishing the Imamate in the Shiite sense were nowhere near fulfilment.

Yet there was practically no way to refuse al-Ma'mûn's invitation. The caliph was then living at Merv, in Transoxiana. The Imam, living in Medina in Arabia and occupied, like his predecessors, with teaching his disciples and performing acts of piety, was forced to leave his family and close companions and embark on the long journey to Merv. It took three months.

We shall return later to what happened during the rest of this journey and to how it ended. For now, we should remember that the Imam's younger sister, named Fâtima, like the Prophet's daughter from whom the line of Imams descended, set out some time afterward to join her brother. Her long route passed through Qomm. There she fell ill and died at the age of sixteen. This is the origin of the shrine dedicated to the young woman whom Shiite devotion calls Ma'sûmeh, “the Immaculate,” and who for more than eleven centuries has drawn the fervent devotion of Iranians, always eager to undertake long pilgrimages.

Perhaps we begin to sense the secret of Qomm when, in the first light of the morning sun, we gaze on the immense façade of its celebrated shrine, rising in a single sweep of enamelled tiles whose deep blue merges high above with the blue of the sky. We then recall that the land of Iran has been called “sky-coloured” (âsmân-gûn). Alongside that image we should set another: the shrine at Jam-Karân, some six or ten kilometres south of Qomm, dedicated to the Hidden Imam, “the Imam of our time.”
We shall speak of this sanctuary later (Book VII).

On the roads leading to these holy places we can be certain that we are following in the footsteps of those who went before us: Qâzî Sa'îd, certainly, and long before him Ibn Bâbûyeh, whose work Qâzî Sa'îd's commentary would make resonate so powerfully.

Let us recall briefly who Ibn Bâbûyeh was. The ending of his name corresponds in Persian to the ending -oê in Pahlavi words; the pronunciation “Babawaih” is simply its Arabic form. He came from a distinguished Shiite family of Qomm; his father and brother were also celebrated scholars. The name Sadûq, meaning “the utterly truthful,” by which he is most often known, had already been given to his father. The two are therefore sometimes distinguished as Sadûq I, the father, and Sadûq II, the son.

Of the distinguished 'Alî ibn Hosayn ibn Bâbûyeh Qommî, Sadûq I, we shall recall only what bears on his son's life and reveals how thoroughly the Imam's followers were accustomed to the supernatural. Shaykh Sadûq I had travelled to Arab Iraq, where he held long conversations with Abû'l-Qâsim Hosayn ibn Rûh, the third of the four successive representatives (nâ'ib) of the Hidden Imam during the Lesser Occultation (ghaybat soghrâ). He asked this representative to deliver a letter requesting that the Imam pray for him to have a son.

Word came from the Imam that he had granted the request and that the shaykh would have two sons: one, Abû Ja'far, was the Sadûq with whom we are chiefly concerned here, Sadûq II; the other was Abû 'Abdallah Hosayn. For this reason, Shaykh Sadûq II used to say that it was through the Imam's prayers that he had come into the world.

Another version says that his father had earlier received a letter from the Eleventh Imam, Hasan al-'Askarî, father of the Hidden Imam (see Book VII), giving him the same assurance. The historian Tonkabonî believes that the two accounts can readily be reconciled . Shaykh Sadûq I died in Qomm in 329/940, the very year in which the Twelfth Imam's “Greater Occultation” (Ghaybat kobrâ) began.

In a final letter that year, the Imam had informed his fourth and last representative, 'Alî ibn Mohammad al-Samarrî, that he must appoint no successor, and it was then that this representative died, entrusting everything to God. Shortly beforehand, at a Shiite gathering in Baghdad, 'Alî al-Samarrî had astonished those present by announcing that 'Alî ibn Hosayn ibn Bâbûyeh had died that very day in Qomm. A week or two later, travellers arriving from Qomm confirmed that the death had occurred at precisely the hour announced by the Imam's representative.

As for Sadûq II, the figure who concerns us here and whom we shall simply call Ibn Bâbûyeh or Shaykh Sadûq, his exact birth date is unknown. We have only a latest possible date: before 329/940. He died in 381/991 and was buried at Ray, a few kilometres south of modern Tehran, near the shrine of Shah 'Abdol-'Azîm, where pilgrims still faithfully visit his tomb.

We know that in 355/956 he was in Baghdad, surrounded by Shiites eager to hear him. We even possess the record of a major conference on the Imamate held in the presence of the Buyid prince Roknoddîn . The shaykh taught celebrated pupils, including Shaykh Mofîd and Ibn Shâdhân, and Shiite writers are unstinting in their praise of him.

His writings were indeed extensive: bibliographers list more than two hundred titles. Only the most important have survived and are periodically republished in Iran. Most consist of the hadîth and akhbâr, the traditions and reports handed down from the Imams. Sadûq was among those to whom we owe the preservation of this vast body of material, in which we hear the Imams themselves instructing their close followers. Their teaching, as we have seen, went far beyond fiqh, the science of religious law: it embraced the highest questions of spiritual philosophy and the inner life, and from the beginning it gave Shiite Islam its distinctive character.

We shall mention only a few of the most famous titles. 1) Man lâ yahzoro'l-faqîh, “The Book of the Man Who Has No Doctor at Hand”—in other words, “The Book of the Man Who Is His Own Doctor.” The title may imitate that of a work by the famous physician Rhazes, who likewise died at Ray, around 313/925, and wrote a “Book of the Man Who Is His Own Physician.”

2) The great collection 'Oyûn akhbâr al-Imâm al-Rezâ, or “Sources for the History of Imam al-Rezâ,” a work of fundamental importance for the history and understanding of the Seventh and Eighth Imams. It preserves accounts of extraordinary debates attended by representatives of all the religions then in existence. 3) Kitâb al-I'tiqâdât, a book setting out the Shiite profession of faith; it contains thoroughly Platonic teachings on the soul's pre-existence and descent.

4) Finally, the great Kitâb al-Tawhîd, a collection of the Imams' traditions dealing with everything involved in affirming the divine Oneness (tawhîd). It shows how the teaching concerning the Imams is the only possible “affirmative” or cataphatic theology compatible with the apophatic theology—the via negationis, or tanzîh—required by the affirmation of divine unity. This is the book on which Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî wrote his masterly commentary, comparable to Mollâ Sadrâ's commentary on Kolaynî's Kâfî. These are two monuments of Shiite spiritual philosophy.
Thus we find ourselves in Qomm once again, some seven centuries later, with our philosopher.

Qâzî Sa'îd was born there, then, in 1049/1639. His father, Mohammad Mofîd Qommî, was himself a hakîm, a sage or philosopher. Young Sa'îd naturally began his studies in Qomm, then came to Isfahan around 1068/1658, where his principal teachers, as we noted above, were Mollâ Rajab 'Alî Tabrîzî and Mollâ Mohsen Fayz Kâshânî, the most famous pupil of Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî .

In his youth he had also studied medicine. He had an elder brother, Mohammad Hosayn, just as gifted as himself, who had also studied under Rajab 'Alî Tabrîzî and who, besides writing a major Persian commentary on the Qur'an, was an expert in medicine. To distinguish Sa'id from his brother, people nicknamed him Hakîm kutchak—something like the younger philosopher.
The Safavid ruler Shah 'Abbâs II (who reigned from 1052/1642 to 1077/1677) likewise treated him with great respect, as did the members of his court, and appointed him to judicial office.

Hence the title under which he is generally cited: Qâzî (Qâdî) Sa'îd Qommî, Judge Sa'îd of Qomm. He spent most of his life in Qomm, teaching and receiving visits from thinkers and other notable figures who came to consult him.

Nevertheless, we find evidence of frequent journeys between Qomm and Isfahan, a distance of only about 250 kilometres. Between 1084/1673 and 1088/1677 he was certainly in Qomm, where several of his writings are dated.

But he was in Isfahan in 1093/1682, for the manuscript of the first volume of his great commentary on Sadûq's Tawhîd was copied there on his instructions, reviewed in full by him, and annotated in his own hand, with the date Rajab 1093/July 1682. He was also in Isfahan between 1099/1688 and 1102/1691, when he wrote the Arba'înîyât and his commentary on the Tradition of the White Cloud, while continuing work on the Tawhîd commentary. Apart from this we have many scattered autobiographical remarks in his writings, but they chiefly concern his inner spiritual life. He died in Qomm in 1103/1691–1692.

As we can see, we know rather little about the outward circumstances of our philosopher's life. As with all his fellow thinkers, his real life is in his work; it is there that we must look for clues to the path he followed. The works are not lacking in references to dreams and waking visions or to particular events, but these belong above all to his spiritual autobiography.

What is certain is that the teachings of his two masters, Mohsen Fayz Kâshânî and Rajab 'Alî Tabrîzî, shaped his thought together. The first awakened his deep inclination towards what we might call a Shiite ishrâqî philosophy of illumination, grounded almost entirely in the traditions of the holy Imams. Mohsen Fayz, himself a mystical philosopher and a prolific author of some two hundred books and treatises in Arabic and Persian, was an akhbârî . Qâzî Sa'îd, too, was an akhbârî philosopher.

We shall return later (Book VI) to the centuries-old opposition between the akhbârîs and the osûlîs. For now, leaving other considerations aside, let us say only that the former, as represented by such figures as Mohsen Fayz and his pupils, appear as Shiite spiritual philosophers who insist on taking the traditions in their entirety. They accept all the reports transmitted from the Imams instead of submitting them to the often rationalistic criticism practised by others. Through ta'wîl 'irfânî, spiritual and mystical interpretation, they can discern the hidden meaning of traditions that rationalistic theology dismisses as incomprehensible or absurd.

From his other teacher, Rajab 'Alî Tabrîzî, Qâzî Sa'îd inherited a firm and original position on the metaphysics of being, one he shared with the other pupils of that teacher: his own brother Mohammad Hosayn, 'Abbâs Mawlawî, and others. This position denies that there can be any analogy of being—or of any attribute whatever—between the Necessary Being and a being that has a beginning. It is neither nominalism nor agnosticism.

Rather, it expresses the conviction that the uncompromising demand of Tawhîd, divine Oneness, can be met only by negative or apophatic theology, which denies every Name and qualification of the transcendent divine Essence. At the same time, this negative theology establishes both the necessity and the meaning of divine manifestations, or theophanies.

The works themselves have this distinctive feature: although conceived on an ambitious scale, they remained unfinished, as did many writings of Mîr Dâmâd. Even so, their extent is considerable. We shall chiefly mention the following.

1) Kalîd-e behesht (The Key to Paradise) is a short work written in Persian , in which Qâzî Sa'îd outlines the fundamental theses of his metaphysics, the ideas underlying all his writings. In agreement with his teacher Rajab 'Alî Tabrîzî, he argues that the word “being” cannot have a common meaning (ishtirâk ma'nawî) when applied, on the one hand, to the Being that is Necessary in itself (Wâjib al-wojûd) and, on the other, to a being that is not necessary in itself (momkin al-wojûd) . The two uses of the word share only a verbal form (ishtirâk lafzî): they are, in fact, homonyms. For the Necessary transcends being and every category of being.
Indeed, this supreme philosophical reality lies beyond even metaphysics ('ilm ilâhî), the discipline that studies being (wojûd) as found in what exists (mawjûd).

We shall return to this point, for this fundamental thesis governs how negative or apophatic theology is connected with the idea of divine manifestations and, consequently, with the whole spiritual understanding of the Imams.

2) The Kitâb al-Arba'în, a “Commentary on Forty Hadiths,” written by Qâzî Sa'îd when he was thirty years old. Unfortunately it remained unfinished: the commentary reaches only the twenty-eighth tradition, with a gap after the eighteenth. Collections of “forty hadiths” form a whole literature of their own. Their inspiration is a saying of the Prophet promising special glory on the Day of Resurrection to anyone who preserves for the community forty traditions suited to its religious needs .

Within Shiism this became a pious way for an individual to bring together the teachings that answered his own theological or devotional concerns, while presenting them as an anthology of authoritative texts received from the Imams. Several traditions in Qâzî Sa'îd's unfinished collection reappear in his great commentary on the Tawhîd. It seems that, increasingly absorbed by this second and overwhelming task, he could no longer pursue the first. He refers to his earlier commentary on many occasions, and scholars need to read the two together: both are dense and richly documented.

3) The Kitâb al-Arba'înîyat, or Book of Forty Treatises. The words completing its title explain its purpose: “for the unveiling of the Lights of the hieratic world.” Once again we meet the number forty, with its evident mystical significance. This work must not be confused with the previous one. Here too, however, Qâzî Sa'îd was unable to complete his plan. He wrote ten treatises between 1089/1670 and 1102/1690–91.

The first sets out a spiritual interpretation (ta'wîl) of the canonical Prayer (Salât), its inward meaning, and belongs alongside another treatise on the same subject that we shall mention below . The tenth is entitled al-Talâ'i' (“The Vanguard” or “The Scouts”) or al-Bawâriq al-malakûtîya (“Flashes of Lightning in the Malakût”). In it the author addresses several philosophical problems by the methods of spiritual knowledge ('irfân). He recalls a spiritual vision he experienced in Qomm and refers to his teachers and contemporaries. Begun in Isfahan in 1095/1684, the treatise was incorporated into the Arba'înîyât collection in Safar 1102/November 1690.

We have some reason, however, to think that another work by Qâzî Sa'îd, the Commentary on the Narrative of the White Cloud (Sharh hadîth al-ghamâma), forms an eleventh work in this collection, which in any case remained incomplete. In principle it could also have belonged to the preceding collection, despite its length. There therefore seems no need to list it separately in his bibliography.
